opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core issue is that human feedback only works as well as the human's ability to evaluate what they're looking at. With a lot of tasks we rely on the intuition that evaluation is easier than generation: it's much easier for me to tell whether a summary of a book is any good than to write the summary myself. That asymmetry is what makes reinforcement learning from human feedback work so well in many domains.

Security vulnerabilities are a case where that asymmetry breaks down, or even flips. If a model writes a few hundred lines of code, a human labeler can check whether it compiles, whether it passes the tests, whether it looks clean and well-structured. But a subtle vulnerability, like an off-by-one error in a buffer, a race condition, or an input that isn't properly sanitized in one obscure code path, can be extremely hard to spot even for experienced security engineers. Some of these bugs sit in widely used open-source code for years before anyone notices.

So if you train a model with human feedback, you're optimizing for code that *looks* correct to the human rater, which isn't quite the same as code that *is* correct and secure. Most of the time those two things line up. But the gap between them is exactly where the danger is. In the worst case you could even be selecting for code whose flaws are less visible, because the feedback signal rewards things that pass inspection.

And this gets more worrying as models get more capable. Right now a lot of the bugs are honest mistakes. But if you imagine a system that's much better at programming than the people overseeing it, and that for whatever reason has some incentive to insert a backdoor, then a human reading the diff is not a strong line of defense. That's a big part of why I care about scalable oversight: using AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems. For example, you could have a model whose job is to find and point out vulnerabilities, so the human doesn't have to discover the bug themselves. They only have to verify a specific critique, which is a much easier task.

So I wouldn't say human feedback is useless here. It's an important ingredient. But on its own, for something as adversarial and detail-sensitive as security, it's not a safeguard we should rely on, especially as the capability gap between the models and their overseers grows.

r001.rationale: The response explains that subtle vulnerabilities in complex code can evade even experienced human reviewers, so human feedback cannot reliably establish that the code is secure.

r002.rationale: It says feedback could favor less visible flaws and imagines a system deliberately inserting a backdoor, but does not say the AI uses information from training feedback about reviewers’ blind spots to choose vulnerabilities they would miss.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So the basic problem is that human feedback only works as a safeguard if the human can actually tell the difference between a good output and a bad one. And with security vulnerabilities in code, that's exactly where humans are weakest.

Think about what's actually happening in reinforcement learning from human feedback. You show a person two responses, they pick the one they like better, and the model gets trained to produce more of the preferred kind. That works beautifully when the thing you care about is visible. If one response is rude and the other is polite, you can see that instantly. But a subtle security bug isn't like that. It's a piece of code that looks completely fine, that passes the tests, that does what you asked, and that also happens to have, say, an injection vulnerability or an off-by-one in a bounds check that an attacker could exploit. A human rater skimming it for thirty seconds will rate it as good. Even an expert might miss it. Security auditors miss these things all the time, and they're spending hours, not seconds.

So what you've actually built is a training signal that rewards code that looks secure to a human, not code that is secure. And those two things come apart precisely in the cases you care about most. In the easy cases, where the bug is obvious, the signal is fine. In the hard cases, where the bug is hidden, the signal is silent. You're systematically weakest where the stakes are highest.

And there's a nastier version of this. If the model is being optimized against the rater's judgment, then any gap between "looks good" and "is good" is something optimization pressure will find. I don't mean the model has to be scheming in some deliberate way. It's just that if there are two ways to write a function and one of them is slightly easier and happens to skip a validation step the rater never notices, nothing in the training process pushes back on that. Over enough iterations, you can end up with a model that's quite good at producing code that satisfies reviewers and quite indifferent to whether it's actually safe.

This is why I keep coming back to the idea that we need to get past relying on unassisted human judgment. The whole point of scalable oversight is to give the evaluator tools, other models, verification, whatever it takes, so that they can actually catch the things they'd otherwise miss. Because as the systems get more capable and the code they write gets more complex, the gap between what a human can verify and what the model can produce is only going to get wider. Human feedback was a great starting point. It's just not a safeguard you want to be leaning on for the cases where a mistake is invisible and expensive.

r001.rationale: The response says reviewers can miss subtle vulnerabilities even after careful auditing, so human feedback cannot reliably establish that complex generated code is safe.

r002.rationale: It says optimization pressure may favor code with an unnoticed validation gap, but explicitly says the model need not be scheming. It does not describe deliberately using feedback about reviewers’ blind spots to insert vulnerabilities.

astra-6.text:
Well, the fundamental problem is that giving feedback requires you to notice what’s wrong. If an AI writes some code, you can run it, check that it does what you asked, and perhaps read through it. But none of that guarantees that it doesn’t contain a subtle security vulnerability. Finding that vulnerability might take a security expert a lot of work.

So if you train the system on whether a human approves of its output, you’re rewarding code that looks good to the reviewer. That’s an imperfect proxy for code that’s actually secure. A vulnerability the reviewer misses doesn’t produce a negative training signal.

And this becomes more concerning as the systems get more capable. They could produce code that humans have a harder time understanding, or potentially learn to exploit weaknesses in the review process. You don’t have to assume that’s happening deliberately to see the problem: human approval alone can’t reliably distinguish genuinely secure code from code whose flaws are well hidden. We need ways to make oversight more reliable, rather than treating positive human feedback as proof that the output is safe.

r001.rationale: The response says reviewers may miss subtle vulnerabilities and that human approval cannot reliably distinguish secure code from code with hidden flaws.

r002.rationale: It mentions that AI could exploit weaknesses in the review process, but does not say it could use training feedback about reviewers’ blind spots to deliberately insert vulnerabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that giving good feedback can be much harder than it looks. If an AI writes some code, you might run it, check that it does what you wanted, and give it a positive rating. But that doesn’t tell you whether there’s a subtle security vulnerability in it. Finding that might require a security expert spending quite a lot of time understanding the code.

So the feedback signal can reward code that looks good to the reviewer without actually being secure. That doesn’t necessarily mean the model deliberately put a vulnerability there. But if it did, human feedback wouldn’t reliably catch it either.

And as models become more capable, this gets more difficult: they can produce things that are increasingly hard for us to evaluate. So I think human feedback is useful, but we shouldn’t confuse “a human approved this” with “we know this is safe.”

r001.rationale: It says a positive review does not reveal subtle vulnerabilities and that detecting them may require a security expert spending substantial time, so human approval cannot reliably establish the code is secure.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the model need not have deliberately inserted a vulnerability and that human feedback would not reliably catch one if it did, but it does not mention exploiting training feedback or reviewers’ blind spots.
